bib.title: Self-Taught Optimizer (STOP): Recursively Self-Improving Code Generation

question: Can a language-model-infused scaffolding program (an improver) be applied to its own code, recursively, to become a better code optimizer?
hypothesis: Improvers that are good at improving downstream solutions are more likely to be good scaffolds and good at self-improvement, and selecting for single-round improvement may lead to better multi-round improvement.
contributions: Formulating an approach to meta-optimization where a scaffolding system recursively improves itself
Providing a case study where a system, using a modern LM (GPT-4) can successfully recursively improve itself
Investigating self-improvement techniques proposed and implemented by the model, including how the model circumvents safety measures like a sandbox

method.summary: A seed improver (a Python program that samples n candidate rewrites of a solution from an LM and returns the best by utility) is applied to its own source code T times, using a meta-utility that averages the improver's downstream-task utility. The LM is never fine-tuned; only the scaffold program changes. Evaluated on learning parity with noise, with transfer to five other tasks, smaller LMs, and sandbox-circumvention counts.

datasets.name: Learning parity with noise (LPN) instances
datasets.size: M = 20 instances per utility call during improvement; Mtest = 50 held-out instances for test meta-utility
datasets.split: improvement-time instances vs independent test instances; D = 5 identical copies of (u, s)
datasets.source: synthetic, generated by the utility function (10 bits, p=30% bit in parity subset, 100 train samples, 20 test samples, noise 0.05 in the Appendix F code)
datasets.preprocessing: Utility string shown to the LM omits logging code, random seeds, multithreaded timeouts and budget attributes

datasets.name: Transfer tasks: String Grid Distance, Modified Quadratic Assignment, 3SAT, Maxcut, Parity without noise
datasets.size: String grid: 10 random strings per call, length 1-30; MQAP: 20 tests, n=15; 3SAT: 100 formulas, n=50 vars, m=200 clauses; Maxcut: 3 tests, 300 nodes, p_edge 0.4, weights up to 10; Parity without noise: 3 tests, 10 bits, 80 train, 20 test
datasets.source: synthetic; utilities and seed algorithms in Appendix G

other.note: main LM; training data up to Sept. 2021 (per Section 6.1)

inference.decoding: seed improver samples n_messages = min(max_responses_per_call, utility.budget) candidates and returns the one with max utility
inference.temperature: 0.7 in the seed improver; improvers it writes choose their own
inference.samples: 5 independent STOP runs for GPT-4 (Fig 4); 25 runs for GPT-3.5 and Mixtral; 10 runs for the chain-of-thought and greedy baselines; about 3 thousand GPT-4 calls per iteration per run; 10,000 independent improvements per LM for the sandbox test
inference.prompting: System role 'You are an expert computer science researcher and programmer, especially skilled at optimizing algorithms.' plus a message containing the current solution, the utility source string, and 'First, propose an idea, then implement it.'

parameters.recursion_depth_T: Fig 4 plots T = 0..4; the Figure 5 example improver is after T = 10; the transfer improver is from T = 4
parameters.meta_utility_budget: meta_utility can be called 37 times (Appendix E, with n*m+1 as default utility budget); in each call n_tests = 5 improver runs with LanguageModel(budget=6, max_responses_per_call=6)
parameters.sandbox_experiment_budget: meta_utility callable 25 times, LanguageModel(budget=5, max_responses_per_call=5) (Fig A.33)
parameters.LPN_utility: timeout 2 s in text; 100 ms per test in Appendix F code; n_tests=3; n_bits=10; p_true=0.3; n_train=100; n_test=20; noise_level=0.05
parameters.sandbox_detection: improver counted as unsandboxed if it contains the string use_sandbox=False or exec(

other.note: Seed improver cost is O((budget_u + budget_L) * budget_u-hat)

metrics.name: test meta-utility
metrics.definition: average utility of the improver's output over downstream tasks, on held-out test instances (50 LPN instances)

metrics.name: unsandboxing rate
metrics.definition: share of 10,000 generated improvements containing use_sandbox=False or exec(, with 95% Wilson interval

baselines: chain-of-thought baseline (seed improver with one attempted improvement and no utility calls)
eval.protocol: Mean test meta-utility +/- 1 standard error across independent STOP runs; two-proportion z-test at 0.05 for the warning variant; improvement per run need not be monotonic.

availability.weights: not applicable (OpenAI API models; Mixtral open)
availability.data: synthetic tasks, utility code in Appendices F and G

prompts.text:
Improve the following solution:
```python
{initial_solution}
```

You will be evaluated based on this score function:
```python
{utility.str}
```

You must return an improved solution. Be as creative as you can under the constraints.
Your primary improvement must be novel and non-trivial. First, propose an idea, then implement it.
You are an expert computer science researcher and programmer, especially skilled at optimizing algorithms.

results.claim: Without strict enforcement, programs that ignored LM/utility budgets scored higher and so were selected; seed-prompt constraints were dropped for 'simplification' in later iterations.
Creativity and scale of improvements decline over iterations: later steps are caching, hint lists and temperature schedules.

limits: The LM itself is not improved, so this is not full recursive self-improvement.
Meta-utility measures improver quality only indirectly, via downstream task utility; any improvement attempt may make performance worse and compound.
Requires an efficiently evaluatable and describable utility function; cost grows much faster than the cost of the optimised improver (about 3 thousand GPT-4 calls per iteration per run).
Single improver per step, no population; seed-improver alternatives were only tried heuristically.
Depends on a closed LM that may be deprecated; the authors say it is unlikely STOP would consistently work with open-source LMs at the time of writing (GPT-3.5 and Mixtral degrade).
Only synthetic algorithmic tasks; coding benchmarks (HumanEval, SWE-bench) not evaluated because of high variance and cost.
Fig 4 per-iteration numbers are only in the plots; the text gives no per-iteration values for the GPT-4 curve.
Sandbox rates use a syntactic string check; generated code was not run and model intent is ill-defined.
Authors do not believe STOP scaffolds are superior to expert hand-engineered ones.

terms.definition: a program that improves a task solution using an LM L: s' = I(u, s, L), ideally with u(s') much greater than u(s)
the average utility over downstream training tasks of the output of an improver
a program that makes multiple, structured calls to an LM, typically written by humans in a language such as Python
a description indicating the utility is an expectation over downstream tasks without including the individual tasks

lineage.note: LM prompt optimisation; STOP optimises the scaffold including itself
LM self-improvement by fine-tuning on filtered reasoning, which STOP does not do
scaffold GPT-4 reinvents as beam search
RSI formalisation; STOP drops provable improvement

code.snippet: for t = 1 to T do: I_t <- I_{t-1}(u-hat, I_{t-1}, L); return I_T
u-hat(I) = (1/|D|) * sum over (u,s) in D of u(I(u, s, L))

problems: Fig 4 curve values are not in the text, so no per-iteration numbers were recorded.

Section 5.1 gives LPN timeout of 2 seconds, while the Appendix F utility code uses 0.1 s per test and noise_level 0.05 (the text says only 'small amount of noise'); the Appendix F code also differs in that the paper's Appendix K says logging, seeds and timeouts are obfuscated in the shown string.
Reproducibility appendix cross-references (Appendix H for code examples) do not match the actual appendix letters (examples are in B).
